frames.narration: A request reaches the frontend. Dapper's library there makes the sampling decision once: this request is one of the 1 in 1,024 that will be traced. It creates a root span with a new 64-bit trace id and no parent, and puts the trace context where code in this thread and its callbacks can reach it.

The frontend calls the search service. The RPC library creates a child span, with its own span id and the frontend's span id as parent, and sends the trace id, span id and the sampled flag along with the call. No application code is involved.

messages.label: RPC + trace id, span id, sampled

frames.narration: The search service sees the sampled flag and records its own side of the span without flipping a coin. The client and the server each add annotations to the same span, such as when the request was sent and when it was received. An unsampled request would have written nothing.

Each process writes its finished spans to a local log file on its own host. This is cheap, about 426 bytes per span on average in the report, and happens outside the request, so the user is not kept waiting for it.
A Dapper daemon on each host reads the log files and sends the spans to the collection pipeline. It runs at the lowest scheduler priority and used at most 0.3% of one core in the report's worst case.

The spans are written to a regional Bigtable repository. A whole trace is one row and each span is a column, which suits Bigtable's sparse layout because traces have any number of spans. The median delay from process to repository is under 15 seconds, though the 98th percentile can be hours.

messages.label: write spans into the trace's row

frames.narration: An engineer opens the trace through the repository API. The tree is rebuilt from the ids alone, and it shows each service's span with its timing, so the slow branch is easy to spot. If one host's log has not arrived yet, its branch is simply missing until it does.

messages.label: trace tree for the slow request
